title: Ὅρκος καὶ Γόος
titleEn: The Oath and the Mourning — Iliad 19.238–337
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: The gifts are carried from Agamemnon's hut into the assembly, Briseis among the women. Agamemnon lifts his hands to Zeus and swears that he never touched her, and Talthybius throws the slaughtered boar into the sea. Achilles blames Zeus for the bewilderments sent to men, and dismisses the army to eat. The Myrmidons carry the gifts to his ship; Briseis finds Patroclus dead and laments him, and the women groan with her. The elders beg Achilles to eat, but he refuses until sunset, keeps Agamemnon, Menelaus, Odysseus, Nestor, Idomeneus and Phoenix beside him in his grief, and speaks to the dead Patroclus: his heart is fasting for longing, and he thinks of his father in Phthia and his son on Scyros.

sentences.t:
ἦ, καὶ Νέστορος υἷας ὀπάσσατο κυδαλίμοιο
Φυλεΐδην τε Μέγητα Θόαντά τε Μηριόνην τε
καὶ Κρειοντιάδην Λυκομήδεα καὶ Μελάνιππον·
sentences.tr:
ē, kai Nestoros huias opassato kydalimoio
Phyleïdēn te Megēta Thoanta te Mērionēn te
kai Kreiontiadēn Lykomēdea kai Melanippon·
sentences.i: So he said, and took with him the sons of glorious Nestor, and Meges, son of Phyleus, and Thoas and Meriones, and Lycomedes, son of Creon, and Melanippus;
sentences.n: The speaker is Odysseus, who has just ended his advice to Achilles and now carries out Agamemnon’s order (19.193–195) to choose young men to fetch the gifts. ἦ, καί ‘he spoke, and’ is a stock opening. ὀπάσσατο, aorist middle of ὀπάζω, is ‘took along as followers’. κυδαλίμοιο ‘glorious’ goes with Νέστορος. Φυλεΐδην ‘son of Phyleus’ and Κρειοντιάδην ‘son of Creon’ are patronymics. A puzzle: the line says ‘the sons of Nestor’, but the five men then named are not Nestor’s sons anywhere in the poem, so either Nestor’s sons are a first group to which the five are added, or the line is imperfect; the English decides nothing.

sentences.t: βὰν δ’ ἴμεν ἐς κλισίην Ἀγαμέμνονος Ἀτρεΐδαο.
sentences.tr: ban d’ imen es klisiēn Agamemnonos Atreïdao.
sentences.l: They set out to go to the hut of Agamemnon, Atreus’-son.
sentences.i: And they set out to go to the hut of Agamemnon, son of Atreus.
sentences.n: βὰν is the aorist 3rd plural of βαίνω without the augment (= Attic ἔβησαν); βῆ δ’ ἴμεν ‘set out to go’ is a stock phrase of the poem, and ἴμεν is the epic infinitive of εἶμι (= Attic ἰέναι). The subject is the men Odysseus picked. Ἀτρεΐδαο is the epic genitive of the patronymic Ἀτρεΐδης ‘son of Atreus’.

sentences.t: αὐτίκ’ ἔπειθ’ ἅμα μῦθος ἔην, τετέλεστο δὲ ἔργον·
sentences.tr: autik’ epeith’ hama mythos eēn, tetelesto de ergon·
sentences.l: Straightway then together there was the word, and the deed was accomplished;
sentences.i: Then at once the word and the deed went together, and the work was done;
sentences.n: The line is a short saying: ἅμα ‘together’ joins μῦθος ‘word’ with ἔργον ‘deed’, and ἔην is the epic imperfect of εἰμί ‘was’ (= Attic ἦν). τετέλεστο is the pluperfect passive of τελέω ‘accomplish’, ‘had been accomplished’. Nothing is said of the walk to the hut: the tale moves straight to the gifts being carried out.

sentences.t:
ἑπτὰ μὲν ἐκ κλισίης τρίποδας φέρον, οὕς οἱ ὑπέστη,
αἴθωνας δὲ λέβητας ἐείκοσι, δώδεκα δ’ ἵππους·
sentences.tr:
hepta men ek klisiēs tripodas pheron, hous hoi hypestē,
aithōnas de lebētas eeikosi, dōdeka d’ hippous·
sentences.l:
Seven tripods from the hut they carried, which he had undertaken to give him,
and fire-bright cauldrons, twenty, and twelve horses;
sentences.i: They carried seven tripods out of the hut, which he had undertaken to give him, and twenty fire-bright cauldrons, and twelve horses;
sentences.n: The gifts are the ones Agamemnon’s offer named; line 244 is word for word the line at 9.123, where they were first listed, and keeps that English. φέρον is an unaugmented imperfect ‘carried’. οὕς οἱ ὑπέστη is a relative clause: ὑπέστη, aorist of ὑφίσταμαι, is ‘undertook, promised’, and οἱ is ‘to him’, that is Achilles. αἴθωνας ‘fire-bright’ is the epithet of the cauldrons, translated every time.

sentences.t:
ἐκ δ’ ἄγον αἶψα γυναῖκας ἀμύμονα ἔργα ἰδυίας
ἕπτ’, ἀτὰρ ὀγδοάτην Βρισηΐδα καλλιπάρῃον.
sentences.tr:
ek d’ agon aipsa gynaikas amymona erga iduias
hept’, atar ogdoatēn Brisēïda kalliparēion.
sentences.l:
and out they led quickly women knowing blameless works,
seven, and as eighth Briseis, fair-cheeked.
sentences.i: and they quickly led out seven women skilled in blameless crafts, and, as the eighth, Briseis, fair-cheeked.
sentences.n: ἐκ … ἄγον ‘led out’ is a verb split by tmesis. ἰδυίας is the epic feminine perfect participle of οἶδα ‘know’, so ‘knowing blameless works’ means skilled in crafts such as weaving; the exact sense of ἀμύμων is not known, and ‘blameless’ is the traditional rendering. ἀτάρ here only continues the count, ‘and’. ὀγδοάτην is an epic form of ‘eighth’. Βρισηΐδα καλλιπάρῃον ‘Briseis, fair-cheeked’ is her stock epithet, translated every time.

sentences.t:
χρυσοῦ δὲ στήσας Ὀδυσεὺς δέκα πάντα τάλαντα
ἦρχ’, ἅμα δ’ ἄλλοι δῶρα φέρον κούρητες Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
chrysou de stēsas Odyseus deka panta talanta
ērch’, hama d’ alloi dōra pheron kourētes Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
And of gold, having weighed, Odysseus ten talents in all
led the way, and together others bore gifts, the young men of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: Odysseus weighed out ten talents of gold in all and led the way, and the other young men of the Achaeans carried gifts along with him.
sentences.n: στήσας (aorist participle of ἵστημι) with τάλαντα is ‘having set the talents in the balance’ and so ‘weighed out’. τάλαντα is a weight, kept as ‘talents’; πάντα goes with it, ‘ten talents in all’. ἦρχ’ is ἦρχε, from ἄρχω ‘lead’, here ‘led the way’. ἄλλοι ‘others’ goes with κούρητες. κούρητες is an epic plural of κοῦρος ‘young man’; here it means the picked young men (the same word is also a people’s name, which is not meant here).

sentences.t:
καὶ τὰ μὲν ἐν μέσσῃ ἀγορῇ θέσαν, ἂν δ’ Ἀγαμέμνων
ἵστατο·
sentences.tr:
kai ta men en messēi agorēi thesan, an d’ Agamemnōn
histato·
sentences.l:
And these in the middle of the assembly they put, and up
stood Agamemnon;
sentences.i: These they set down in the middle of the assembly, and Agamemnon stood up;
sentences.n: τὰ μέν ‘these’ are the gifts. ἂν δ’ … ἵστατο is a verb split by tmesis (ἂν = ἀνά), ‘stood up’; ἵστατο is the imperfect middle of ἵστημι. θέσαν is the aorist 3rd plural of τίθημι without the augment (= Attic ἔθεσαν).

sentences.t:
Ταλθύβιος δὲ θεῷ ἐναλίγκιος αὐδὴν
κάπρον ἔχων ἐν χερσὶ παρίστατο ποιμένι λαῶν.
sentences.tr:
Talthybios de theōi enalinkios audēn
kapron echōn en chersi paristato poimeni laōn.
sentences.l:
and Talthybius, like a god in voice,
a boar holding in his hands, stood beside the shepherd of the people.
sentences.i: and Talthybius, whose voice was like a god’s, stood beside the shepherd of the people, holding a boar in his hands.
sentences.n: Talthybius is the herald, whose voice carries over the assembly. θεῷ ἐναλίγκιος αὐδήν ‘like a god in voice’ is a stock phrase: ἐναλίγκιος ‘like’ takes the dative, and αὐδήν is an accusative of respect, ‘in voice’. παρίστατο is the imperfect middle of παρίστημι ‘stand beside’. ποιμένι λαῶν ‘shepherd of the people’ is the title of a leader, here Agamemnon, translated every time. This unit begins in the middle of line 250.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδης δὲ ἐρυσσάμενος χείρεσσι μάχαιραν,
ἥ οἱ πὰρ ξίφεος μέγα κουλεὸν αἰὲν ἄωρτο,
κάπρου ἀπὸ τρίχας ἀρξάμενος Διὶ χεῖρας ἀνασχὼν
εὔχετο·
sentences.tr:
Atreïdēs de eryssamenos cheiressi machairan,
hē hoi par xipheos mega kouleon aien aōrto,
kaprou apo trichas arxamenos Dii cheiras anaschōn
eucheto·
sentences.l:
And Atreus’-son, drawing with his hands the knife
that always hung beside the great sheath of his sword,
having made first-offering of hairs from the boar, to Zeus his hands raising,
prayed;
sentences.i: Then the son of Atreus drew with his hands the knife that always hung beside the great sheath of his sword, and, making a first offering of hairs from the boar and raising his hands to Zeus, he prayed;
sentences.n: The first two lines are the lines of 3.271–272, where Agamemnon drew the same knife for the oath over the lambs, and they keep that English. ἐρυσσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of ἐρύω ‘draw’. ἄωρτο is a pluperfect passive of ἀείρω, ‘hung’ (= Attic ἤορτο). In κάπρου ἀπὸ τρίχας ἀρξάμενος the preposition is split from the participle (tmesis): ἀπαρξάμενος means ‘making a first offering’, the hairs cut off the victim being the first rite. Διὶ χεῖρας ἀνασχών ‘raising his hands to Zeus’ is the usual gesture of prayer.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἐπ’ αὐτόφιν εἵατο σιγῇ
Ἀργεῖοι κατὰ μοῖραν ἀκούοντες βασιλῆος.
sentences.tr:
toi d’ ara pantes ep’ autophin heiato sigēi
Argeioi kata moiran akouontes basilēos.
sentences.l:
and they, all, on the spot sat in silence,
the Argives, according to what is fitting listening to the king.
sentences.i: and all the Argives sat there in silence, listening as was fitting to their king.
sentences.n: τοί is the epic plural article used as ‘they’. ἐπ’ αὐτόφιν is ‘on the spot, there’: -φιν is an old ending that does the work of a case ending. εἵατο is the epic 3rd plural of ἧμαι ‘sit’. κατὰ μοῖραν ‘as is fitting’ is a stock phrase. Ἀργεῖοι is one of the three names of the army, all used for the same people. ἀκούοντες governs the genitive βασιλῆος, ‘listening to the king’. This unit begins in the middle of line 255.

sentences.t: εὐξάμενος δ’ ἄρα εἶπεν ἰδὼν εἰς οὐρανὸν εὐρύν·
sentences.tr: euxamenos d’ ara eipen idōn eis ouranon euryn·
sentences.l: and having prayed, he then spoke, looking to the wide heaven:
sentences.i: and when he had prayed he spoke, looking up to the wide heaven:
sentences.n: εὐξάμενος is the aorist participle of εὔχομαι ‘pray’ (the same verb as εὔχετο, two lines back); εἶπεν ‘spoke’ opens the oath. ἰδὼν εἰς οὐρανὸν εὐρύν ‘looking up to the wide heaven’ is a stock phrase, translated as at 3.364.

sentences.t:
ἴστω νῦν Ζεὺς πρῶτα θεῶν ὕπατος καὶ ἄριστος
Γῆ τε καὶ Ἠέλιος καὶ Ἐρινύες, αἵ θ’ ὑπὸ γαῖαν
ἀνθρώπους τίνυνται, ὅτις κ’ ἐπίορκον ὀμόσσῃ,
sentences.tr:
istō nyn Zeus prōta theōn hypatos kai aristos
Gē te kai Ēelios kai Erinyes, hai th’ hypo gaian
anthrōpous tinyntai, hotis k’ epiorkon omossēi,
sentences.l:
“Let Zeus now know first, highest and best of the gods,
and Earth and the Sun and the Erinyes, who beneath the earth
punish men, whoever swears a false oath,
sentences.i: “Let Zeus now know first, highest and best of the gods, and Earth and the Sun and the Erinyes, who under the earth punish men, whoever swears a false oath,
sentences.n: ἴστω is the 3rd person imperative of οἶδα ‘know’; in an oath it means ‘let … be witness’, the gods being called to hear what follows. Line 258 is also a line of the Odyssey, in an oath there too, and keeps its English. ὕπατος ‘highest’ and ἄριστος ‘best’ both go with Ζεύς. The Erinyes are the avenging spirits who punish perjury, and Ἠέλιος is the Sun, who sees everything. τίνυνται is a present middle, ‘exact punishment from’, with the accusative ἀνθρώπους. ὅτις κ’ ἐπίορκον ὀμόσσῃ ‘whoever swears a false oath’ is a general relative with the aorist subjunctive; the same words come at 3.279.

sentences.t:
μὴ μὲν ἐγὼ κούρῃ Βρισηΐδι χεῖρ’ ἐπένεικα,
οὔτ’ εὐνῆς πρόφασιν κεχρημένος οὔτέ τευ ἄλλου.
sentences.tr:
mē men egō kourēi Brisēïdi cheir’ epeneika,
out’ eunēs prophasin kechrēmenos oute teu allou.
sentences.l:
that never I on the girl Briseis a hand laid,
neither of a bed, as pretext, needing, nor of anything else,
sentences.i: that I never laid a hand on the girl Briseis, wanting neither a bed as my pretext nor anything else,
sentences.n: μὴ μέν introduces the content of an oath, ‘that I did not’. ἐπένεικα is the aorist of ἐπιφέρω, so χεῖρ’ ἐπένεικα is ‘laid a hand on’. κούρῃ Βρισηΐδι is ‘the girl Briseis’, κούρη being ‘girl, maiden’. κεχρημένος is the perfect participle of χράομαι in its sense ‘need, want’ (+ genitive), and the construction is rough: εὐνῆς ‘of a bed’ is a genitive, the object of κεχρημένος and matched by τευ ἄλλου ‘of anything else’, while πρόφασιν is an accusative that works like an adverb, ‘as a pretext’. The sense is ‘wanting neither a bed, as a pretext, nor anything else’; the line is hard and this is a best reading.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἔμεν’ ἀπροτίμαστος ἐνὶ κλισίῃσιν ἐμῇσιν.
sentences.tr: all’ emen’ aprotimastos eni klisiēisin emēisin.
sentences.l: but to have stayed untouched in my huts.
sentences.i: but that she stayed untouched in my huts.
sentences.n: ἀλλά ‘but’ continues the oath. ἔμεν’ is the elided epic infinitive ἔμεναι ‘to be’, here ‘to have stayed’; after the finite ἐπένεικα the oath changes to an infinitive, and the English smooths the change over. ἀπροτίμαστος is a rare word: the sense ‘untouched’ is the traditional one and fits the context, but how it is built is not clear. κλισίῃσιν ἐμῇσιν ‘in my huts’ is an epic dative plural; the plural stands for the one dwelling.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ τι τῶνδ’ ἐπίορκον ἐμοὶ θεοὶ ἄλγεα δοῖεν
πολλὰ μάλ’, ὅσσα διδοῦσιν ὅτίς σφ’ ἀλίτηται ὀμόσσας.
sentences.tr:
ei de ti tōnd’ epiorkon emoi theoi algea doien
polla mal’, hossa didousin hotis sph’ alitētai omossas.
sentences.l:
But if any of this is a false oath, may the gods give me pains,
very many, as many as they give to whoever sins against them, having sworn.”
sentences.i: But if any of this is a false oath, may the gods give me pains, very many, as many as they give to anyone who offends them by swearing falsely.”
sentences.n: The oath ends with a curse on himself. εἰ δέ τι τῶνδ’ ἐπίορκον ‘but if any of this is a false oath’. δοῖεν is the aorist optative of δίδωμι, an optative of wish, ‘may they give’. πολλὰ μάλ’ ‘very many’ is added to ἄλγεα ‘pains’. In ὅσσα διδοῦσιν ὅτίς σφ’ ἀλίτηται ὀμόσσας ‘as many as they give to whoever sins against them having sworn’, ἀλίτηται is the aorist subjunctive middle of ἀλιταίνω ‘sin against’, σφ’ is σφι ‘them’, and ὅτίς is printed with that accent in the edition. ὀμόσσας is the aorist participle ‘having sworn’, here ‘by swearing falsely’.

sentences.t: ἦ, καὶ ἀπὸ στόμαχον κάπρου τάμε νηλέϊ χαλκῷ.
sentences.tr: ē, kai apo stomachon kaprou tame nēleï chalkōi.
sentences.l: He spoke, and cut the boar’s throat with pitiless bronze.
sentences.i: So he said, and cut the boar’s throat with the pitiless bronze.
sentences.n: ἦ, καί ‘he spoke, and’ closes the oath and begins the act. ἀπὸ … τάμε is a verb split by tmesis (aorist of τάμνω ‘cut’, unaugmented); στόμαχον is ‘throat’. νηλέϊ χαλκῷ ‘pitiless bronze’ is a stock phrase, translated every time; the same words end the line at 3.292.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν Ταλθύβιος πολιῆς ἁλὸς ἐς μέγα λαῖτμα
ῥῖψ’ ἐπιδινήσας βόσιν ἰχθύσιν·
sentences.tr:
ton men Talthybios poliēs halos es mega laitma
rhips’ epidinēsas bosin ichthysin·
sentences.l:
That one Talthybius into the great gulf of the grey sea
flung, whirling it round, as food for the fishes;
sentences.i: Talthybius whirled it round and flung it into the great gulf of the grey sea, to be food for the fish;
sentences.n: τόν ‘that one’ is the dead boar, put first for emphasis. ῥῖψ’ ἐπιδινήσας is ‘whirling it round, flung’; the same pair is used at 3.378 for a helmet. πολιῆς ἁλός ‘of the grey sea’ is a stock phrase; λαῖτμα is a poetic word for the ‘gulf, depth’ of the sea. βόσιν ἰχθύσιν is ‘food for the fishes’, the dative giving who it is for.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀχιλλεὺς
ἀνστὰς Ἀργείοισι φιλοπτολέμοισι μετηύδα·
sentences.tr:
autar Achilleus
anstas Argeioisi philoptolemoisi metēuda·
sentences.l:
but Achilles,
standing up, spoke among the war-loving Argives:
sentences.i: and Achilles stood up and spoke among the war-loving Argives:
sentences.n: αὐτάρ ‘but, and’ turns to the next speaker. ἀνστάς is the epic aorist participle of ἀνίστημι, ‘having stood up’. Ἀργείοισι φιλοπτολέμοισι ‘the war-loving Argives’ is an epithet group, translated every time; φιλοπτόλεμος is built from φίλος ‘dear’ and πτόλεμος, an old form of πόλεμος ‘war’. μετηύδα ‘spoke among’ is the verb for addressing a group. This unit begins in the middle of line 268.

sentences.t: Ζεῦ πάτερ ἦ μεγάλας ἄτας ἄνδρεσσι διδοῖσθα·
sentences.tr: Zeu pater ē megalas atas andressi didoistha·
sentences.l: “Father Zeus, truly great bewilderments to men you give;
sentences.i: “Father Zeus, you do indeed give men great bewilderments;
sentences.n: Ζεῦ πάτερ ‘Father Zeus’ opens many speeches; ἦ is the particle ‘truly’. ἄτη is a clouding of the mind that makes a man act wrongly or blindly; ‘bewilderment’ is the house rendering. διδοῖσθα is the epic 2nd singular present of δίδωμι (= Attic δίδως). The speaker is Achilles, and the words are about what Zeus has let Agamemnon do.

sentences.t:
οὐκ ἂν δή ποτε θυμὸν ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ἐμοῖσιν
Ἀτρεΐδης ὤρινε διαμπερές,
sentences.tr:
ouk an dē pote thymon eni stēthessin emoisin
Atreïdēs ōrine diamperes,
sentences.l:
Not at all ever the heart in my breast, mine,
Atreus’-son would have stirred right through,
sentences.i: Never would the son of Atreus have stirred up the heart in my breast so utterly,
sentences.n: οὐκ ἄν … ὤρινε is the past unreal: a past indicative with ἄν (ὤρινε, imperfect or aorist, is the same form in the 3rd singular), ‘would not have stirred’, said of something that did happen. δή ποτε ‘ever’ strengthens it. ὤρινε is from ὀρίνω ‘stir up, rouse’. διαμπερές ‘right through, utterly’ is an adverb. θυμὸν ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ἐμοῖσιν ‘the heart in my breast’ has the epic dative plural στήθεσσιν. The unit ends in the middle of line 272.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ κε κούρην
ἦγεν ἐμεῦ ἀέκοντος ἀμήχανος·
sentences.tr:
oude ke kourēn
ēgen emeu aekontos amēchanos·
sentences.l:
nor would he have taken the girl
with me unwilling, being past all dealing with;
sentences.i: nor would he have taken the girl against my will, impossible to deal with as he is;
sentences.n: κεν … ἦγεν is again the past unreal, ‘would have led away’. ἐμεῦ ἀέκοντος is a genitive absolute, ‘me unwilling’, from ἀέκων. ἀμήχανος, from μηχανή ‘means’, is ‘without resource’ and, said of a person, ‘impossible to deal with’, as at 10.167, 13.726, 15.14 and 16.29; the Odyssey’s ‘helpless’ (19.363) is not used, because said by Achilles of Agamemnon it would ask us to pity him. This unit begins in the middle of line 272.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά ποθι Ζεὺς
ἤθελ’ Ἀχαιοῖσιν θάνατον πολέεσσι γενέσθαι.
νῦν δ’ ἔρχεσθ’ ἐπὶ δεῖπνον, ἵνα ξυνάγωμεν Ἄρηα.
sentences.tr:
alla pothi Zeus
ēthel’ Achaioisin thanaton poleessi genesthai.
nyn d’ erchesth’ epi deipnon, hina xynagōmen Arēa.
sentences.l:
but somewhere Zeus
wished death to come to many Achaeans.
But now go to your meal, so that we may bring Ares together.”
sentences.i: but Zeus, I suppose, wanted death to come to many Achaeans. But now go to your meal, so that we may join battle.”
sentences.n: ποθι (= που) ‘somewhere, I suppose’ softens the claim, as if Achilles were guessing at Zeus’ purpose. ἤθελ’ is the elided imperfect ἤθελε of ἐθέλω (η- is the augmented ἐ-), ‘wished’. θάνατον … γενέσθαι ‘death to come about’ takes the dative of the people, Ἀχαιοῖσιν πολέεσσι, where πολέεσσι is the epic dative plural of πολύς. This unit begins in the middle of line 273. The last line, νῦν δ’ ἔρχεσθ’ ἐπὶ δεῖπνον…, is the same line as 2.381, where Agamemnon sends the army to eat before battle, and it keeps that English; here it closes Achilles’ speech. ἵνα ξυνάγωμεν Ἄρηα is a purpose clause with the aorist subjunctive; Ares stands for battle, ‘bring Ares together’ meaning ‘join battle’.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρ’ ἐφώνησεν, λῦσεν δ’ ἀγορὴν αἰψηρήν.
sentences.tr: hōs ar’ ephōnēsen, lysen d’ agorēn aipsērēn.
sentences.l: So then he declared, and dissolved the hasty assembly.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and broke up the hastily-gathered assembly.
sentences.n: The line is also Odyssey 2.257, at the end of Telemachus’ assembly, and keeps its English. ἐφώνησεν ‘declared, spoke out’; λῦσεν ‘loosed, broke up’; αἰψηρός is ‘hasty, swift’, and the assembly was called in haste.

sentences.t: οἳ μὲν ἄρ’ ἐσκίδναντο ἑὴν ἐπὶ νῆα ἕκαστος,
sentences.tr: hoi men ar’ eskidnanto heēn epi nēa hekastos,
sentences.l: They, then, scattered, each to his own ship,
sentences.i: They scattered, each to his own ship,
sentences.n: The line has the shape of Odyssey 2.258, which also tells of a scattering assembly. ἐσκίδναντο is the imperfect of σκίδναμαι ‘scatter’. ἑήν is the epic possessive ‘his own’, and νῆα is the accusative of νηῦς ‘ship’. οἳ μὲν ἄρ’ ‘they, then’ marks a turn from the speaker to the crowd.

sentences.t:
δῶρα δὲ Μυρμιδόνες μεγαλήτορες ἀμφεπένοντο,
βὰν δ’ ἐπὶ νῆα φέροντες Ἀχιλλῆος θείοιο.
sentences.tr:
dōra de Myrmidones megalētores amphepenonto,
ban d’ epi nēa pherontes Achillēos theioio.
sentences.l:
and the gifts the Myrmidons, great-spirited, busied themselves about,
and went to the ship carrying them of Achilles, the divine.
sentences.i: and the great-spirited Myrmidons busied themselves about the gifts, and went to the ship of divine Achilles, carrying them.
sentences.n: Μυρμιδόνες are Achilles’ own men. μεγαλήτορες ‘great-spirited’ is their stock epithet, translated every time. ἀμφεπένοντο is the imperfect of ἀμφιπένομαι ‘busy oneself about’, with δῶρα as its object. βὰν δ’ ἐπὶ νῆα ‘and went to the ship’ is formulaic; βὰν has no augment. Ἀχιλλῆος θείοιο ‘of divine Achilles’: θεῖος is ‘divine’, kept apart from δῖος ‘heavenly’.

sentences.t:
καὶ τὰ μὲν ἐν κλισίῃσι θέσαν, κάθισαν δὲ γυναῖκας,
ἵππους δ’ εἰς ἀγέλην ἔλασαν θεράποντες ἀγαυοί.
sentences.tr:
kai ta men en klisiēisi thesan, kathisan de gynaikas,
hippous d’ eis agelēn elasan therapontes agauoi.
sentences.l:
And these in the huts they put, and seated the women,
and the horses into the herd drove the attendants, noble ones.
sentences.i: They put the gifts in the huts and seated the women, and the noble attendants drove the horses into the herd.
sentences.n: κάθισαν is the aorist of καθίζω used as a causative, ‘they made (the women) sit’. θέσαν is the unaugmented aorist of τίθημι. θεράποντες ἀγαυοί ‘noble attendants’ is a stock group, translated every time. The women are those led out at 245–246; the horses, the twelve at 244. ἀγέλη is a ‘herd’.

sentences.t:
Βρισηῒς δ’ ἄρ’ ἔπειτ’ ἰκέλη χρυσέῃ Ἀφροδίτῃ
ὡς ἴδε Πάτροκλον δεδαϊγμένον ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ,
sentences.tr:
Brisēïs d’ ar’ epeit’ ikelē chryseēi Aphroditēi
hōs ide Patroklon dedaïgmenon oxeï chalkōi,
sentences.l:
And Briseis then, like golden Aphrodite,
when she saw Patroclus mangled by sharp bronze,
sentences.i: But Briseis, who was like golden Aphrodite, when she saw Patroclus mangled by sharp bronze,
sentences.n: Βρισηῒς is the nominative of the name whose accusative Βρισηΐδα stood at 246; the diaeresis marks the two vowels as separate. ἰκέλη ‘like’ takes the dative: ἰκέλη χρυσέῃ Ἀφροδίτῃ ‘like golden Aphrodite’ is a stock comparison for beauty, translated every time. ὡς ἴδε ‘when she saw’: ὡς is ‘when’ and ἴδε is the aorist of ὁράω. δεδαϊγμένον is the perfect passive participle of δαΐζω ‘tear, mangle’. ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ ‘sharp bronze’ is a stock phrase, translated every time. The sentence is not finished: the main verb comes in the next line.

sentences.t:
ἀμφ’ αὐτῷ χυμένη λίγ’ ἐκώκυε, χερσὶ δ’ ἄμυσσε
στήθεά τ’ ἠδ’ ἁπαλὴν δειρὴν ἰδὲ καλὰ πρόσωπα.
sentences.tr:
amph’ autōi chymenē lig’ ekōkye, chersi d’ amysse
stēthea t’ ēd’ hapalēn deirēn ide kala prosōpa.
sentences.l:
about him pouring herself, was crying out clearly, and with her hands tore
her breast and her soft neck and her fair face.
sentences.i: threw herself about him and cried out in a clear voice, and tore with her hands at her breast and her soft neck and her fair face.
sentences.n: ἀμφ’ αὐτῷ χυμένη ‘pouring herself about him’: χυμένη is the epic aorist middle participle of χέω ‘pour’, here ‘flinging herself down’. ἐκώκυε is the imperfect of κωκύω ‘cry out’, and λίγ’ is the neuter accusative of λιγύς used as an adverb, ‘clearly’, that is in a clear, carrying voice. ἄμυσσε is the imperfect of ἀμύσσω ‘tear, scratch’. The three objects are στήθεα ‘breast’, δειρήν ‘neck’ and πρόσωπα; the last is a neuter plural, but it is used of one face, ‘her fair face’. The ‘breast’ is plural in Greek and singular here.

sentences.t: εἶπε δ’ ἄρα κλαίουσα γυνὴ ἐϊκυῖα θεῇσι·
sentences.tr: eipe d’ ara klaiousa gynē eïkuia theēisi·
sentences.l: and she spoke, weeping, the woman like goddesses:
sentences.i: and, weeping, the woman, like goddesses, spoke:
sentences.n: εἶπε is the aorist of λέγω ‘spoke’. γυνὴ ἐϊκυῖα θεῇσι ‘the woman like goddesses’ is a stock phrase: ἐϊκυῖα is the feminine perfect participle of ἔοικα ‘be like’ and takes the dative; θεῇσι is the epic dative plural of θεά ‘goddess’. κλαίουσα ‘weeping’ is a present participle. A speech follows.

sentences.t:
Πάτροκλέ μοι δειλῇ πλεῖστον κεχαρισμένε θυμῷ
ζωὸν μέν σε ἔλειπον ἐγὼ κλισίηθεν ἰοῦσα,
sentences.tr:
Patrokle moi deilēi pleiston kecharismene thymōi
zōon men se eleipon egō klisiēthen iousa,
sentences.l:
“Patroclus, to me, miserable, made most welcome to my heart,
alive I left you, I from the hut going,
sentences.i: “Patroclus, dearest to my heart, miserable as I am, you were alive when I left you, going away from the hut,
sentences.n: The speech is Briseis’ lament, and the vocative Πάτροκλε opens it. μοι δειλῇ ‘to me, miserable’ is a dative of the person feeling, with δειλῇ feminine and agreeing with μοι. πλεῖστον κεχαρισμένε θυμῷ ‘made most welcome to my heart’ is the stock address ‘dear to my heart’ (5.243), with the superlative πλεῖστον added. ἔλειπον is the imperfect of λείπω ‘leave’. κλισίηθεν ‘from the hut’ has the ending -θεν, which means ‘from’. ἰοῦσα is the participle of εἶμι ‘go’.

sentences.t:
νῦν δέ σε τεθνηῶτα κιχάνομαι ὄρχαμε λαῶν
ἂψ ἀνιοῦσ’·
sentences.tr:
nyn de se tethnēōta kichanomai orchame laōn
aps anious’·
sentences.l:
but now you dead I find, leader of the people,
back coming up;
sentences.i: but now, as I come back, I find you dead, leader of the people;
sentences.n: νῦν δέ ‘but now’ turns the sentence. τεθνηῶτα is the epic perfect participle of θνῄσκω ‘die’, ‘dead’. κιχάνομαι ‘I come upon, find’ is a present middle. ὄρχαμε λαῶν ‘leader of the people’ is a stock vocative, translated every time. ἂψ ἀνιοῦσ’ ‘coming back up’ is ἀνιοῦσα, from ἄνειμι, elided; ἂψ is ‘back’. This unit ends in the middle of line 290.

sentences.t: ὥς μοι δέχεται κακὸν ἐκ κακοῦ αἰεί.
sentences.tr: hōs moi dechetai kakon ek kakou aiei.
sentences.l: so for me receives evil after evil always.
sentences.i: so it is for me: evil always follows on evil.
sentences.n: ὥς here is ‘so, thus’. δέχεται, from δέχομαι ‘receive, take up’, has the sense that one evil takes over from another, ‘evil receives evil’; the Greek does not say more than this, and the English is a plain reading of it. κακὸν ἐκ κακοῦ ‘evil after evil’. αἰεί ‘always’ is the epic form of Attic ἀεί. This unit begins in the middle of line 290.

sentences.t:
ἄνδρα μὲν ᾧ ἔδοσάν με πατὴρ καὶ πότνια μήτηρ
εἶδον πρὸ πτόλιος δεδαϊγμένον ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ,
sentences.tr:
andra men hōi edosan me patēr kai potnia mētēr
eidon pro ptolios dedaïgmenon oxeï chalkōi,
sentences.l:
The husband to whom my father and lady mother gave me
I saw before the city mangled by sharp bronze,
sentences.i: The husband to whom my father and my lady mother gave me I saw before the city, mangled by sharp bronze,
sentences.n: ἄνδρα is the object of εἶδον, put first for emphasis; ᾧ ἔδοσάν με is a relative clause, ‘to whom they gave me’, with ἔδοσαν the aorist 3rd plural of δίδωμι. πότνια μήτηρ ‘lady mother’ is a stock phrase for a revered mother, translated every time. πρὸ πτόλιος ‘before the city’ has the epic genitive πτόλιος (= Attic πόλεως). δεδαϊγμένον ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ is the same phrase as in line 283.

sentences.t:
τρεῖς τε κασιγνήτους, τούς μοι μία γείνατο μήτηρ,
κηδείους, οἳ πάντες ὀλέθριον ἦμαρ ἐπέσπον.
sentences.tr:
treis te kasignētous, tous moi mia geinato mētēr,
kēdeious, hoi pantes olethrion ēmar epespon.
sentences.l:
and three brothers, whom one mother bore to me,
beloved, who all met the day of destruction.
sentences.i: and three brothers, whom one mother bore for me, dear to me, who all met their day of destruction.
sentences.n: κασιγνήτους ‘brothers’ continues as object of εἶδον. τούς μοι μία γείνατο μήτηρ ‘whom one mother bore to me’: γείνατο is the aorist middle of γείνομαι ‘beget, bear’, and μία ‘one’ means ‘the same’. κηδείους is ‘dear, close’ (people one cares for), in apposition. ὀλέθριον ἦμαρ ἐπέσπον: ἐπέσπον is the aorist of ἐφέπω, ‘came up to, met’, and ὀλέθριον ἦμαρ is ‘the day of destruction’, that is, the day they were killed.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ μὲν οὐδέ μ’ ἔασκες, ὅτ’ ἄνδρ’ ἐμὸν ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεὺς
ἔκτεινεν, πέρσεν δὲ πόλιν θείοιο Μύνητος,
κλαίειν,
sentences.tr:
oude men oude m’ easkes, hot’ andr’ emon ōkys Achilleus
ekteinen, persen de polin theioio Mynētos,
klaiein,
sentences.l:
Nor yet, not even, did you keep allowing me, when my husband swift Achilles
killed, and sacked the city of divine Mynes,
to weep,
sentences.i: Nor would you ever let me weep, when swift Achilles killed my husband and sacked the city of divine Mynes,
sentences.n: οὐδὲ μὲν οὐδέ is a strong double negative, ‘not even’. ἔασκες is the iterative imperfect of ἐάω ‘allow’: ‘you kept allowing’ (so in the literal line; ‘would let’ in the free English), said of the time after the husband’s death; the infinitive κλαίειν ‘to weep’ comes at the end of the unit. ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς ‘swift Achilles’ is a short form of the usual epithet, translated every time. πέρσεν is the aorist of πέρθω ‘sack’, unaugmented. θείοιο Μύνητος ‘divine Mynes’: Mynes is named again at 2.692, struck down in the same sack; the line does not say how he stood to her. This unit ends in the middle of line 297.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά μ’ ἔφασκες Ἀχιλλῆος θείοιο
κουριδίην ἄλοχον θήσειν, ἄξειν τ’ ἐνὶ νηυσὶν
ἐς Φθίην, δαίσειν δὲ γάμον μετὰ Μυρμιδόνεσσι.
sentences.tr:
alla m’ ephaskes Achillēos theioio
kouridiēn alochon thēsein, axein t’ eni nēusin
es Phthiēn, daisein de gamon meta Myrmidonessi.
sentences.l:
but you kept saying that you would make me of Achilles, the divine,
the wedded wife, and would take me in the ships
to Phthia, and hold a wedding-feast among the Myrmidons.
sentences.i: but you kept saying that you would make me the wedded wife of divine Achilles, and take me in the ships to Phthia, and hold the wedding-feast among the Myrmidons.
sentences.n: ἔφασκες is an iterative imperfect of φημί: ‘you used to say’. The infinitives θήσειν, ἄξειν and δαίσειν are future infinitives after it, ‘that you would make … take … hold’. κουριδίην ἄλοχον ‘wedded wife’ is a stock phrase, translated every time. Φθίην is Achilles’ home. δαίσειν γάμον is ‘to give a wedding-feast’. Μυρμιδόνεσσι is the epic dative plural. This unit begins in the middle of line 297.

sentences.t: τώ σ’ ἄμοτον κλαίω τεθνηότα μείλιχον αἰεί.
sentences.tr: tō s’ amoton klaiō tethnēota meilichon aiei.
sentences.l: Therefore I weep for you without ceasing, dead, always gentle.”
sentences.i: Therefore I weep for you without ceasing, now that you are dead, you who were always gentle.”
sentences.n: τώ ‘therefore’ is the old instrumental of the article (= Attic τῷ). ἄμοτον is an adverb ‘insatiably, unceasingly’. κλαίω σε τεθνηότα ‘I weep for you dead’ takes the perfect participle τεθνηότα in agreement with σε. μείλιχον αἰεί ‘always gentle’: μείλιχος is ‘gentle, soothing’, and the word agrees with σε, so the gentleness is Patroclus’.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατο κλαίουσ’, ἐπὶ δὲ στενάχοντο γυναῖκες
Πάτροκλον πρόφασιν, σφῶν δ’ αὐτῶν κήδε’ ἑκάστη.
sentences.tr:
hōs ephato klaious’, epi de stenachonto gynaikes
Patroklon prophasin, sphōn d’ autōn kēde’ hekastē.
sentences.l:
So she spoke weeping, and groaned in answer the women
for Patroclus as pretext, but their own sorrows each.
sentences.i: So she spoke, weeping, and the women groaned in answer, mourning Patroclus as their pretext, but each her own sorrows.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατο ‘so she spoke’ is the usual close of a speech. ἐπὶ δὲ στενάχοντο ‘and in answer they groaned’: ἐπί is an adverb ‘in addition, in answer’. Πάτροκλον πρόφασιν ‘Patroclus as a pretext’ is in apposition: they wept openly for Patroclus but really for their own sorrows. κήδεα are ‘sorrows’. ἑκάστη ‘each’ is feminine, each of the women.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸν δ’ ἀμφὶ γέροντες Ἀχαιῶν ἠγερέθοντο
λισσόμενοι δειπνῆσαι·
sentences.tr:
auton d’ amphi gerontes Achaiōn ēgerethonto
lissomenoi deipnēsai·
sentences.l:
And around him the elders of the Achaeans were gathering,
beseeching him to dine;
sentences.i: And the elders of the Achaeans gathered around him, begging him to take a meal;
sentences.n: αὐτόν ‘him’ is Achilles. ἀμφὶ … ἠγερέθοντο is a verb split by tmesis, ‘gathered round’; ἠγερέθοντο is an epic imperfect of ἀγείρω. γέροντες Ἀχαιῶν are the elders (the chiefs). λισσόμενοι ‘begging’ is a present participle; δειπνῆσαι is an aorist infinitive ‘to take a meal’. The unit ends in the middle of line 304.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ἠρνεῖτο στεναχίζων·
sentences.tr: ho d’ ērneito stenachizōn·
sentences.l: but he refused, groaning:
sentences.i: but he refused, groaning:
sentences.n: ὃ δέ ‘but he’ is Achilles. ἠρνεῖτο is the imperfect of ἀρνέομαι ‘refuse’, and στεναχίζων ‘groaning’ is a present participle. The unit begins in the middle of line 304; a speech follows.

sentences.t:
λίσσομαι, εἴ τις ἔμοιγε φίλων ἐπιπείθεθ’ ἑταίρων,
μή με πρὶν σίτοιο κελεύετε μηδὲ ποτῆτος
ἄσασθαι φίλον ἦτορ, ἐπεί μ’ ἄχος αἰνὸν ἱκάνει·
sentences.tr:
lissomai, ei tis emoige philōn epipeitheth’ hetairōn,
mē me prin sitoio keleuete mēde potētos
asasthai philon ētor, epei m’ achos ainon hikanei·
sentences.i: “I beg you, if any of my dear companions will listen to me, do not tell me to sate my heart with food and drink before then, since a fearsome grief has come upon me;
sentences.n: λίσσομαι ‘I beg’ is a present middle. εἴ τις … ἐπιπείθεθ’ is a 3rd singular, ἐπιπείθεται ‘obeys, heeds’, with its ending elided: before the rough breathing of ἑταίρων the elided τ’ is written θ’, which is why the form looks odd; ἔμοιγε is ‘me, at least’. μή … κελεύετε is a prohibition with the present imperative, ‘do not bid’. ἄσασθαι is the aorist infinitive of ἄω ‘satisfy oneself with’ (+ genitive σίτοιο μηδὲ ποτῆτος ‘food or drink’). πρίν here is ‘before (that time)’. ἄχος αἰνόν ‘fearsome grief’, as at 4.169. ἱκάνει ‘comes upon’.

sentences.t: δύντα δ’ ἐς ἠέλιον μενέω καὶ τλήσομαι ἔμπης.
sentences.tr: dynta d’ es ēelion meneō kai tlēsomai empēs.
sentences.l: But until the sun has set I shall stay and endure all the same.”
sentences.i: but until the sun has set I shall hold out and endure, all the same.”
sentences.n: δύντα ἐς ἠέλιον is ‘until the sun going down’: δύντα, aorist participle of δύω, agrees with ἠέλιον, and ἐς means ‘until’. μενέω is a future ‘I shall stay’. τλήσομαι ‘I shall endure’ is the future of τλῆναι. ἔμπης ‘all the same, nevertheless’.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ἄλλους μὲν ἀπεσκέδασεν βασιλῆας,
sentences.tr: hōs eipōn allous men apeskedasen basilēas,
sentences.l: So having spoken, the other kings he dispersed,
sentences.i: So he spoke, and sent the other kings away,
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ is a stock phrase. ἀπεσκέδασεν is the aorist of ἀποσκεδάννυμι ‘scatter, send away’. The subject is Achilles; βασιλῆας are the chiefs who had gathered round him.

sentences.t:
δοιὼ δ’ Ἀτρεΐδα μενέτην καὶ δῖος Ὀδυσσεὺς
Νέστωρ Ἰδομενεύς τε γέρων θ’ ἱππηλάτα Φοῖνιξ
τέρποντες πυκινῶς ἀκαχήμενον·
sentences.tr:
doiō d’ Atreïda menetēn kai dios Odysseus
Nestōr Idomeneus te gerōn th’ hippēlata Phoinix
terpontes pykinōs akachēmenon·
sentences.i: but the two sons of Atreus stayed, and heavenly Odysseus, Nestor and Idomeneus and Phoenix, the old horse-driver, trying to cheer him, sorely grieved as he was;
sentences.n: δοιὼ Ἀτρεΐδα ‘the two sons of Atreus’ (Agamemnon and Menelaus) are dual. μενέτην is the dual imperfect of μένω without the augment, ‘the two stayed’, and the verb stands before the further names. δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς ‘heavenly Odysseus’ is a stock epithet, translated every time. γέρων ἱππηλάτα Φοῖνιξ ‘the old man, horse-driver Phoenix’ is a stock phrase, translated every time. τέρποντες ‘cheering’ is a present participle of the active τέρπω, and ἀκαχήμενον is a perfect participle of ἄχομαι ‘be grieved’. πυκινῶς ‘thickly’ could go with either participle; it is taken with ἀκαχήμενον, as in the Odyssey’s πυκινῶς ἀκαχήμενος (20.84), ‘sorely grieved’. The unit ends in the middle of line 312.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τι θυμῷ
τέρπετο, πρὶν πολέμου στόμα δύμεναι αἱματόεντος.
sentences.tr:
oude ti thymōi
terpeto, prin polemou stoma dymenai haimatoentos.
sentences.l:
and not at all in his heart
was he cheered, before to enter the mouth of bloody war.
sentences.i: but he took no cheer in his heart until he should go into the mouth of bloody war.
sentences.n: οὐδέ τι ‘not at all’. τέρπετο is the imperfect middle of τέρπω, ‘took pleasure, was cheered’, the middle of the verb just before. πρὶν … δύμεναι ‘before going into’: δύμεναι is the epic infinitive of δύω ‘enter’. πολέμου στόμα is ‘the mouth of war’, the front of the fighting where it opens on the men. αἱματόεντος ‘bloody’ is the genitive of αἱματόεις. This unit begins in the middle of line 312.

sentences.t: μνησάμενος δ’ ἁδινῶς ἀνενείκατο φώνησέν τε·
sentences.tr: mnēsamenos d’ hadinōs aneneikato phōnēsen te·
sentences.l: And having remembered, heavily he drew up, and spoke:
sentences.i: And remembering him, he heaved a heavy sigh and spoke:
sentences.n: μνησάμενος is the aorist middle participle of μιμνῄσκω ‘remember’; the object, Patroclus, is not named. ἁδινῶς ‘heavily’ is the adverb; ἁδινός is ‘thick, crowded’. ἀνενείκατο is the aorist middle of ἀναφέρω ‘bring up, lift’: the Greek does not say what he lifted, and ‘heaved a sigh’ is the sense that fits. φώνησέν τε ‘and spoke’. A speech follows.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥά νύ μοί ποτε καὶ σὺ δυσάμμορε φίλταθ’ ἑταίρων
αὐτὸς ἐνὶ κλισίῃ λαρὸν παρὰ δεῖπνον ἔθηκας
αἶψα καὶ ὀτραλέως, ὁπότε σπερχοίατ’ Ἀχαιοὶ
Τρωσὶν ἐφ’ ἱπποδάμοισι φέρειν πολύδακρυν Ἄρηα.
sentences.tr:
ē rha ny moi pote kai sy dysammore philtath’ hetairōn
autos eni klisiēi laron para deipnon ethēkas
aipsa kai otraleōs, hopote sperchoiat’ Achaioi
Trōsin eph’ hippodamoisi pherein polydakryn Arēa.
sentences.l:
“Truly, then, once you also, ill-fated, dearest of companions,
yourself in the hut a tasty meal set beside me
quickly and promptly, whenever the Achaeans were hastening
to bring against the horse-taming Trojans tearful Ares.
sentences.i: “Truly, ill-fated one, dearest of my companions, you too once set a tasty meal before me yourself in the hut quickly and promptly, whenever the Achaeans were hastening to bring tearful battle against the Trojans, tamers of horses.
sentences.n: ἦ ῥά νυ ‘truly then’ marks the opening of a tender memory. δυσάμμορε is a vocative, from δυσ- ‘ill’ and ἄμμορος ‘without a share’, so ‘ill-fated, unlucky’. φίλταθ’ ἑταίρων ‘dearest of companions’ is a superlative with the genitive. αὐτός ‘yourself’. λαρὸν δεῖπνον: λαρός is ‘tasty’; its exact sense is not known. παρὰ … ἔθηκας is a verb split by tmesis, ‘set beside, set before’; the dative μοι ‘for me’ is in the first line. αἶψα καὶ ὀτραλέως ‘quickly and promptly’. ὁπότε σπερχοίατ’ is a general condition in the past, ‘whenever they were in a hurry’, with the optative of σπέρχομαι ‘hasten’. Line 318 is word for word 8.516, spoken by Hector to the Trojans, and keeps that English. Τρωσὶν ἐφ’ ἱπποδάμοισι ‘against the horse-taming Trojans’ and πολύδακρυν Ἄρηα ‘tearful Ares’ (that is, battle) are stock phrases, translated every time.

sentences.t:
νῦν δὲ σὺ μὲν κεῖσαι δεδαϊγμένος, αὐτὰρ ἐμὸν κῆρ
ἄκμηνον πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος, ἔνδον ἐόντων,
σῇ ποθῇ·
sentences.tr:
nyn de sy men keisai dedaïgmenos, autar emon kēr
akmēnon posios kai edētyos, endon eontōn,
sēi pothēi·
sentences.i: But now you lie mangled, and my heart goes without drink and food, though they are here within, out of longing for you;
sentences.n: νῦν δέ ‘but now’ sets the present against the past of the line before. κεῖσαι is the 2nd singular of κεῖμαι ‘lie’. δεδαϊγμένος ‘mangled’ is the same participle as in line 283. ἄκμηνον ‘fasting’ is an adjective in agreement with κῆρ ‘heart’; it is a rare word, and the sense is from the context. πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος ‘from drink and food’ is a genitive of what he lacks. ἔνδον ἐόντων is a genitive absolute, ‘they being within’. ποθή is ‘longing’, in the dative (σῇ ποθῇ ‘for longing for you’).

sentences.t:
οὐ μὲν γάρ τι κακώτερον ἄλλο πάθοιμι,
οὐδ’ εἴ κεν τοῦ πατρὸς ἀποφθιμένοιο πυθοίμην,
sentences.tr:
ou men gar ti kakōteron allo pathoimi,
oud’ ei ken tou patros apophthimenoio pythoimēn,
sentences.l:
for no other thing worse could I suffer,
not even if of my father dead I should hear,
sentences.i: for I could suffer nothing worse, not even if I were to hear that my father was dead,
sentences.n: οὐ μὲν γάρ τι … ἄλλο ‘for not any other thing’. κακώτερον is the comparative ‘worse’. πάθοιμι is the aorist optative of πάσχω ‘suffer’, a potential optative. οὐδ’ εἰ … πυθοίμην ‘not even if I were to hear’: πυθοίμην is the aorist optative of πυνθάνομαι. τοῦ πατρὸς ἀποφθιμένοιο is the genitive of the person heard about, with a participle, ‘of his father having died’ (it is not a genitive absolute). This unit begins in the middle of line 321.

sentences.t:
ὅς που νῦν Φθίηφι τέρεν κατὰ δάκρυον εἴβει
χήτεϊ τοιοῦδ’ υἷος· ὃ δ’ ἀλλοδαπῷ ἐνὶ δήμῳ
εἵνεκα ῥιγεδανῆς Ἑλένης Τρωσὶν πολεμίζω·
sentences.tr:
hos pou nyn Phthiēphi teren kata dakryon eibei
chēteï toioud’ huios· ho d’ allodapōi eni dēmōi
heineka rhigedanēs Helenēs Trōsin polemizō·
sentences.i: who now, I suppose, in Phthia sheds a tender tear for want of such a son, while I in a foreign land make war on the Trojans for the sake of horrible Helen;
sentences.n: ὅς … εἴβει is a relative clause about the father, Peleus: που ‘somewhere, I suppose’ makes it a guess. Φθίηφι has the old ending -φι, here ‘in Phthia’. κατὰ … εἴβει is a verb split by tmesis, ‘lets fall’; τέρεν is ‘tender’. χήτεϊ ‘for lack of’ takes the genitive υἷος ‘son’. ὃ δέ ‘but I’ turns to the speaker, who is the ‘I’ of πολεμίζω. ἀλλοδαπῷ ἐνὶ δήμῳ ‘in a foreign land’. ῥιγεδανῆς is a rare word of uncertain sense, probably linked to ῥῖγος ‘shudder, cold’ and meaning ‘horrible’; the exact meaning is not known. Τρωσὶν πολεμίζω ‘I make war on the Trojans’.

sentences.t:
ἠὲ τὸν ὃς Σκύρῳ μοι ἔνι τρέφεται φίλος υἱός,
εἴ που ἔτι ζώει γε Νεοπτόλεμος θεοειδής.
sentences.tr:
ēe ton hos Skyrōi moi eni trephetai philos huios,
ei pou eti zōei ge Neoptolemos theoeidēs.
sentences.l:
or for him who in Scyros is being reared for me, my dear son,
if still somewhere he lives, Neoptolemus, godlike in form.
sentences.i: or if I were to hear of him who is being brought up for me on Scyros, my dear son, if Neoptolemus, godlike in form, is still alive.
sentences.n: ἠέ ‘or’ continues the supposed case of οὐδ’ εἰ … πυθοίμην above, so that the verb is ‘if I were to hear’. τὸν ὅς … τρέφεται is ‘him who is being reared’, with τρέφεται a present passive. Σκύρῳ is Scyros, an island where Achilles’ son is being brought up. εἴ που ἔτι ζώει ‘if he is still alive somewhere’. Νεοπτόλεμος θεοειδής ‘Neoptolemus, godlike in form’; θεοειδής is a stock epithet, translated every time.

sentences.t:
πρὶν μὲν γάρ μοι θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ἐώλπει
οἶον ἐμὲ φθίσεσθαι ἀπ’ Ἄργεος ἱπποβότοιο
αὐτοῦ ἐνὶ Τροίῃ, σὲ δέ τε Φθίην δὲ νέεσθαι,
sentences.tr:
prin men gar moi thymos eni stēthessin eōlpei
oion eme phthisesthai ap’ Argeos hippobotoio
autou eni Troiēi, se de te Phthiēn de neesthai,
sentences.l:
For until now the heart in my breast was hoping
that I alone would perish, far from horse-pasturing Argos,
right here in Troy, and that you to Phthia would return,
sentences.i: For until now the heart in my breast was hoping that I alone would perish here in Troy, far from horse-pasturing Argos, and that you would go back to Phthia,
sentences.n: πρὶν μὲν γάρ ‘for until now, formerly’. ἐώλπει is the pluperfect (used as imperfect) of ἔλπομαι ‘hope’. οἶον ἐμέ ‘I alone’; φθίσεσθαι is a future infinitive ‘would perish’. ἱπποβότοιο ‘horse-pasturing’ is the stock epithet of Argos, translated every time; Argos here is the Greek homeland. αὐτοῦ ‘on the spot, right here’. σὲ δέ τε … νέεσθαι: ‘and that you would return’, with νέεσθαι the epic infinitive of νέομαι. Φθίην δέ, written as two words, is ‘to Phthia’, the -δε ending marking the goal.

sentences.t:
ὡς ἄν μοι τὸν παῖδα θοῇ ἐνὶ νηῒ μελαίνῃ
Σκυρόθεν ἐξαγάγοις καί οἱ δείξειας ἕκαστα
κτῆσιν ἐμὴν δμῶάς τε καὶ ὑψερεφὲς μέγα δῶμα.
sentences.tr:
hōs an moi ton paida thoēi eni nēï melainēi
Skyrothen exagagois kai hoi deixeias hekasta
ktēsin emēn dmōas te kai hypserephes mega dōma.
sentences.l:
so that you might bring my son in a swift black ship
out of Scyros and show him each thing,
my property and my maidservants and my high-roofed great house.
sentences.i: so that you might bring my son away from Scyros in a swift black ship and show him everything: my property and my maidservants and my great high-roofed house.
sentences.n: ὡς ἄν … ἐξαγάγοις is a purpose clause with the optative, ‘so that you might lead out’. θοῇ ἐνὶ νηῒ μελαίνῃ ‘in a swift black ship’ is a stock phrase, translated every time. Σκυρόθεν has the ending -θεν, ‘from Scyros’. δείξειας is an aorist optative ‘show’; ἕκαστα is ‘each thing’. κτῆσιν ἐμήν ‘my property’, δμῶάς ‘maidservants’ (accusative plural of δμωή, printed with the two vowels apart), and ὑψερεφὲς μέγα δῶμα ‘my great high-roofed house’: ὑψερεφής is ‘high-roofed’.

sentences.t:
ἤδη γὰρ Πηλῆά γ’ ὀΐομαι ἢ κατὰ πάμπαν
τεθνάμεν,
sentences.tr:
ēdē gar Pēlēa g’ oïomai ē kata pampan
tethnamen,
sentences.l:
For now Peleus I think either entirely
to be dead,
sentences.i: For now I think that Peleus is either quite dead,
sentences.n: ἤδη γάρ ‘for already, for by now’. ὀΐομαι ‘I think’ takes an accusative and infinitive, Πηλῆα … τεθνάμεν, with τεθνάμεν the epic perfect infinitive of θνῄσκω ‘to be dead’. κατὰ πάμπαν is ‘altogether’. The unit ends in the middle of line 335.

sentences.t:
ἤ που τυτθὸν ἔτι ζώοντ’ ἀκάχησθαι
γήραΐ τε στυγερῷ καὶ ἐμὴν ποτιδέγμενον αἰεὶ
λυγρὴν ἀγγελίην, ὅτ’ ἀποφθιμένοιο πύθηται.
sentences.tr:
ē pou tytthon eti zōont’ akachēsthai
gēraï te stygerōi kai emēn potidegmenon aiei
lygrēn angeliēn, hot’ apophthimenoio pythētai.
sentences.l:
or perhaps, a little while still living, to be grieved
by hateful old age, and awaiting always my
grievous news, when of me dead he learns.”
sentences.i: or perhaps, still living a little while, he is grieved by hateful old age and always waiting for my grievous news, for the time when he learns that I have perished.”
sentences.n: ἤ που ‘or perhaps’. τυτθὸν ἔτι ζώοντ’ ‘still living for a little’: τυτθόν is a neuter adverb. ἀκάχησθαι is the epic perfect infinitive of ἄχομαι ‘be grieved’, and takes the dative γήραΐ … στυγερῷ ‘by hateful old age’. ποτιδέγμενον is the epic form of προσδεχόμενος ‘waiting for’; its object is ἐμὴν … ἀγγελίην λυγρήν ‘my grievous news’. ὅτ’ ἀποφθιμένοιο πύθηται: the aorist subjunctive πύθηται ‘he learns’ takes the genitive of the person, ἀποφθιμένοιο ‘of me, having perished’, the ‘me’ being understood. This unit begins in the middle of line 335.
